\title{Localization Tells You Where to Read Out a Shortcut, Not Where to Retrain It}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Sonu Akash, Sidhant Holla, Siddhant Khurdiya, Piyush Shiv}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Department of Computer Science and Engineering (AI \& ML)\\
PES University, Bengaluru, India}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Interpretability tools can show where a behaviour happens inside a language model. Is that also where it should be
fixed? We study this for a shortcut learned during fine-tuning, in a setting where the ground truth is known: GPT-2
small learns IMDB sentiment while an invented actor name, planted in 5\% of the training reviews, always comes with the
same label. The logit lens, block swaps and activation patching agree that the name takes over the answer only in the
last three blocks, after the model has already worked out the true sentiment. Retraining ignores this location: one
epoch on clean data removes the shortcut from any single block, because the clean data shows each name with both
labels, and without these counter-examples no block removes it. Reading the answer out depends on it: carrying the
layer-9 state forward to the output removes \pSixBEqLNineRemovedFullFTRange{} of the shortcut across seeds at an
accuracy cost of \pSixBEqLNineDropFullFTRange, while the same dose taken from layer 3 or 6 removes at most
\pSixBEqLSixRemovedFullFTsTwo. LoRA fine-tuning gives the same picture for finding and retraining, and memorized wrong
labels mark where the retraining result stops.
Localization tells us where to read a shortcut out, not where to retrain it.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
shortcut learning, interpretability, logit lens, activation patching, model repair, early exit, GPT-2
\end{IEEEkeywords}
